note: Which document each step owes, and whether it can be evaluated without a person in the
room. flow.json names documents by role and stages by name, and nothing in it joins the
two.
sdlc-flow has seven stages and four documents: explore.md, spec.md, plan.md and
review.md, one per key here. sdlc-spec-audit, sdlc-plan-audit and sdlc-execute own no
document of their own — an audit reports findings against someone else's document, execute
changes the repository. None of that is a file this corpus can hold a brief up against, so
those three are not keys here. Giving them an entry would be inventing an artefact so the
grader has something to read. eval-step.sh exits 2 on a step with no entry here.
sdlc-review owns review.md, the flow's closing document. It owes verification, and it
interviews: its own skill sends a deferred finding, and an unclear one that survives a
second round, to the stakeholder for their word.
`interviews` is the harder fact. sdlc-explore's own skill has
the person describe the idea once and then dispatches a fan-out — the shape of the
gate afterwards is 'anything to add before I dispatch', not a back-and-forth closing open
questions, so evaluating it without a stakeholder in the room is running it as designed.
sdlc-spec is the opposite by its own words: 'brainstorm and spec are one skill because
they are one conversation', run entirely with the person and never dispatched. sdlc-plan
reads as a solo drafting stage but is gated the same way spec is — plan.md is not read by
a worker, it is approved by a person before sdlc-execute may start — so a plan produced
with nobody to approve it would be measuring a stage that never actually finished.
Where a stakeholder is needed, they answer from the brief - what the stakeholder actually
knows - and are given no tools.
